nameStory: Roundleaf thoroughwort gets its common name from its distinctly round or oval leaves, which set it apart from its cousins in the boneset family. The name 'thoroughwort' comes from an old belief that these plants could heal 'thoroughly' - they were considered cure-alls in folk medicine. Early settlers thought anything this widespread and common must be good medicine!
description: Roundleaf thoroughwort is a modest perennial wildflower that grows 2-4 feet tall in New England's wettest places. It produces clusters of small, fuzzy white flowers at the top of its stems in late summer, creating a soft, cloud-like appearance. The plant's most distinctive feature is its round to oval leaves that feel notably soft and velvety to the touch. Unlike many of its boneset relatives, this species prefers the soggiest ground it can find.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Round to oval leaves that feel distinctly soft and fuzzy, almost like velvet, due to fine hairs covering both surfaces. They're arranged in opposite pairs along the stem.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers clustered in flat-topped groups at stem tips, each flower head fuzzy and lacking the typical daisy petals - just fluffy white centers that attract butterflies.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 2-4 feet tall with multiple branching stems from the base, forming loose colonies in wet areas. Stems feel slightly rough and are covered in soft hairs.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces fluffy, dandelion-like seeds with white bristles that catch the wind and float away in fall, leaving behind brown, dried flower heads.

habitat: Look for roundleaf thoroughwort in New England's wettest spots - bogs, wet meadows, marsh edges, and soggy savannas where your feet might sink into the soft ground. It thrives in areas that stay consistently moist or even waterlogged throughout the growing season. You'll often find it growing alongside sedges, cattails, and other moisture-loving plants in low-lying areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy, round leaves on reddish stems. Young plants are easily recognized by their distinctive velvety leaf texture even when small.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and the characteristic round leaves are most prominent. Late summer brings the first white flower clusters at stem tips.
seasonality.fall: White flowers bloom from August through October, followed by fluffy seed heads that disperse on autumn winds. Leaves may yellow before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to the ground, leaving only dried brown stems and empty seed heads that may persist into early winter.

funFact: Despite being in the sunflower family, roundleaf thoroughwort flowers have no petals at all - what looks like tiny white flowers are actually just the fuzzy reproductive parts that most flowers keep hidden in their centers!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with common boneset, but roundleaf thoroughwort's leaves are truly round and separate, while common boneset has pointed leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem. Memory trick: 'Round leaves, wet feet' - if the leaves are round and you're in soggy ground, you've found roundleaf thoroughwort.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'boneset' for this plant family comes from their historical use in treating 'breakbone fever' (dengue), though roundleaf thoroughwort specifically was less commonly used medicinally than its famous cousin, common boneset. Don't confuse thoroughworts with the toxic plant called 'boneset hemp' - stick to visual identification rather than medicinal uses.
compareHints: Among its boneset relatives, roundleaf thoroughwort is the wetland specialist with the roundest, softest leaves. Common boneset has pointed leaves that clasp the stem, while hyssopleaf thoroughwort has narrow, linear leaves. If you're in a bog or wet meadow and the leaves feel like velvet and look perfectly round, you've found the right species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Eupatorium relatives, common boneset is the only one with perfoliate leaves where the stem pierces through the leaf base.

Among the bonesets, hyssopleaf thoroughwort stands out immediately for its extremely narrow leaves—while common boneset has broad, wrinkled leaves that clasp the stem, and rough boneset has lance-shaped leaves, this species looks almost grass-like.

Among the boneset family, rough boneset stands out for its notably hairy, rough-textured leaves and stems, while common boneset has distinctive leaves that appear "perforated" by the stem passing through them.
Among the boneset family, late boneset stands out for its very late bloom time and alternate leaf arrangement.

Among the many boneset species, upland boneset is distinguished by its narrow, stalkless leaves that don't wrap around the stem like common boneset, and its preference for dry habitats unlike most other bonesets.
Unlike common boneset which has leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, New England boneset has clearly separate opposite leaves.
Among the boneset family, tall boneset stands out with its alternate leaf arrangement (most other bonesets have opposite leaves) and its particularly dense, flat-topped flower clusters.
Among its boneset relatives in New England, dogfennel is unmistakable due to its incredibly fine, thread-like leaves - all other Eupatorium species have broad, simple leaves.
Hemp agrimony stands out immediately from all native New England Eupatorium species because of its deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves – every other boneset in our region has simple, undivided leaves.
Unlike common boneset which has distinctive perfoliate leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, Torrey's eupatorium has narrow, separate leaves.
Unlike common boneset with its perforated leaves that wrap around the stem, veined thoroughwort has clearly separate opposite leaves.
